newsitem.title: UK: UK retail sales set to climb again in July.
newsitem.headline: UK retail sales set to climb again in July.

text.p: July retail sales data are expected to show high street spending is thriving as economists look for a strong climb in turnover.
The figures, due out at 0830 GMT on Wednesday, will also be carefully watched for clues as to where and when the Bank of England will move interest rates next.

A Reuters' poll of economists forecast a rise in sales of 0.3 percent month-on-month, down from June's 0.6 percent. But this would push the year-on-year rate of growth up to 5.8 percent from 5.4 in June.

"With the Bank of England keeping a nervous eye on the windfalls, the next few months' retail sales figures will be critical in determining where and when rates peak," said Jonathan Loynes, economist at HSBC Markets.
Windfall payments -- totalling around 35 billion pounds in free shares -- have been received by members of mutually-owned building societies which have converted into banks over the last few months.
These have boosted consumer spending, particularly on large, one-off purchases such as furniture and household goods.
May and June both saw soaring retail sales, much of which was attributed to the windfalls and analysts said they would still have an impact on July sales, although maybe not as large.
"Once the effect of windfalls is past its peak, retail sales volumes will probably fall back," said Michael Saunders, economist at Salomon Brothers.
Economists said anecdotal evidence suggested retail sales remain robust, although survey evidence for July was a little mixed.
The Confederation of British Industry's (CBI) distributive trades survey showed sales growth eased slightly in July.
But a report from the British Retail Consortium (BRC) earlier this month said British retail sales grew at their fastest rate for nine months in July.

"The fine weather in July will have been a positive factor and the survey evidence, while a little mixed, is supportive of another strong performance," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Schroders economist David Philpotts forecast a rise of 0.2 percent but said the chances of a stronger figure were rising every day.
He agreed that growth was still very much dependent on windfall spending and that should be taken into account when assessing the interest rate outlook.

"It's still too early to say whether the strong growth we've seen in recent months is a windfall blip or whether it's part of a wider trend which is still going to be in place once windfalls become less significant."
"This is presumably exactly why the Bank are going to pause for a couple of months now and take stock of how the windfalls have affected consumption," he said.

The Bank of England raised base rates by a 1/4-point on August 7 -- the fourth hike in as many months, taking base rates to seven percent -- and said in last week's inflation report they would now pause to take stock.
But analysts said even disregarding windfall spending, underlying high street activity was robust.

"The fundamentals are still very strong for consumer spending and even it was a windfall blip over the last few months we should still expect reasonably steady growth looking ahead into 1998," Philpotts said.
